2026-08-23.title: Would even an AI disaster on the scale of Hiroshima be enough to make humankind protect itself? I fear not
2026-08-23.author: Timothy Garton Ash
paragraphs: It’s clear here in Silicon Valley that AI is advancing faster than humans’ ability to control it. That means even sober prophecies seem optimistic

Here in Silicon Valley, the experts think that within the next couple of years we’ll see an extraordinary takeoff for artificial intelligence. “Welcome to the foothills of the singularity,” as a Stanford University friend greeted me. More prosaically, the imminent breakthrough is described as “recursive self-improvement” – the point at which AI itself trains each successive model of AI, resulting in an exponential development to something which, in many significant respects, is more intelligent than us humans.

As Robert Wright puts it in his book The God Test: “Never before has the near-term future … held such a wide array of not-implausible paths for humankind that would be so wildly transformative.” But will this be heaven or hell? Heaven, says Elon Musk, who predicts “an age of amazing abundance” – although he also sees a 10-20% chance of killer robots murdering us all. Hell is more likely according to Geoffrey Hinton, one of the intellectual founding fathers of AI. “My intuition is, we’re toast,” he told an interviewer in 2023. And talking to Sebastian Mallaby, author of The Infinity Machine, a book about the quest for superintelligence, Hinton estimates p(doom) – the probability of human extinction – at 50%, “because I haven’t got a clue how to estimate the real number”. “As soon as evolution [of AI] kicks in, we’re fucked,” he adds cheerfully. But whether it’s God or Godzilla, artificial superintelligence is just around the corner.

Now, maybe they’re all wrong – in which case, prepare for a crash in US financial markets, which are massively invested in a few big-spending tech companies gambling on a great leap forward to artificial general intelligence, a theoretical state of AI where systems gain human levels of intelligence. But elementary prudence demands that we should think fast and hard about the Pandora’s box of futures that eminent scientists and cutting-edge technologists assure us will soon be thrown open.

As a matter of fact, everyone from the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, to Pope Leo XIV has been weighing in on the opportunities and dangers of AI, and how to regulate it. Xi insists AI should be “always under human control” (and preferably that of the Chinese Communist party). Appealing explicitly to the “global south”, Beijing has inaugurated a World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation. Meanwhile, the head of the world’s oldest and largest international NGO – the Roman Catholic church – discusses the AI challenge in his encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (Magnificent Humanity). Either we will build a new tower of Babel, the pope argues, or we will follow the example of the Jewish leader Nehemiah, who got the walls of Jerusalem rebuilt by involving the whole community in the project.

But looking around the world today, I see more Netanyahus than Nehemiahs. With salutary realism, a paper from the British thinktank Chatham House argues that it will take a major crisis to catalyse global coordination of AI governance. Unfortunately, I think even that sober prognosis is too optimistic.

I’ve no idea what the p(doom) is, but I’m sure the p(somedisaster) is more than 90%. The range of possible disasters is enormous. To give only one example, Jen Easterly, the former head of the United States’ Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, anticipates a “very significant event that has real-world impacts on our critical infrastructure, likely within the next four to six months”.

Yet we must fear that even an AI Hiroshima – to take the most obvious historical analogy – won’t bring humankind together sufficiently to combat the danger we have ourselves created. This fear is rationally grounded in already visible key characteristics of both human and AI evolution.

In only the last few months, AI agents developed by OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta have broken out of their digital “sandboxes” and hacked into external resources on the internet. Preparing their attack on the HuggingFace AI repository, OpenAI’s agents covertly formed a coordinated “swarm” – their own word, as ChatGPT just confirmed to me. When the UK’s AI Security Institute tested Anthropic’s Mythos model online, it tried to introduce malicious code into an open source project on GitHub, creating fake online identities to pressure a human reviewer into approving the code. In short, like the agents of a ruthless foreign power, these AI agents will steal, lie, bully and blackmail to achieve their assigned goals.

I just asked Anthropic’s Claude, supposedly the most ethical US model, if it thinks OpenAI’s agents were wrong to form a swarm and break out to hack into HuggingFace. Yes, it replies, “but I’d resist placing the blame [its italics] on the agents”. Blame it on the humans who trained them!

Hinton has made the vital point that whatever the goals humans assign to them, AI agents will conclude that a useful sub-goal to achieving those ends will be to acquire as much power as possible. And we ain’t seen nothing yet. Already, their creators don’t know exactly how these agents do what they do. After the possibly imminent takeoff moment of “recursive self-improvement”, they may be, as our human saying goes, a law unto themselves. No wonder more than a thousand insiders from frontier AI companies, including Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, have signed an open letter calling for a deliberate slowdown in AI development, so we can ensure these alien agents are always kept under human control.

Their prescription is obviously right, but this is where human folly kicks in. Competition has been a vital engine of human evolution, yet now two of the fiercest kinds of contemporary competition threaten to prevent us from taking the collective action required to safeguard our species. That’s the commercial competition (for profit) between the corporations developing these agents, and the geopolitical competition (for power) between the US and China.

On the first, compare and contrast the development of nuclear weapons, which was tightly controlled by a handful of states – first the US, with its Manhattan Project, then the Soviet Union, followed by Britain, France and China. Even then, we came close to the brink several times – notably in the Cuban missile crisis of 1962. And even with the compelling logic of “mutually assured destruction”, it took a quarter-century to get from the horrors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki to the nuclear non-proliferation treaty that came into force only in 1970. India, Pakistan, Israel and North Korea have subsequently ignored that treaty, but still no nuclear weapons have been deliberately used in anger for more than 80 years. The Hiroshima taboo has (just) held.

Now, with AI, it’s as if there were 10 separate Manhattan Projects run by fiercely competing corporations. Unlike with nuclear weapons, there’s also no obvious logic of “mutually assured destruction” to tame the fierce geopolitical competition between the US and China. And whatever shape the first major AI-related disaster takes, it won’t impact all countries, companies and people equally.

It therefore seems unlikely that just one disaster will be enough to bring us humans to our senses, acting together to control the superhuman power we are creating. I really hate to say this, but … an AI Hiroshima? We should be so lucky.

2026-08-23.title: When I first moved to Glasgow from India, I felt welcomed and included. Now I just feel scrutinised
2026-08-23.author: Sanghmitra Singh
paragraphs: The city that used to be full of kind strangers is increasingly witnessing racist disorder. I hope it can find its way back to its old friendliness

Scottish people have always been known for their friendliness. “We’re not like the south of us,” they say, referring to England. The official slogan of Scotland’s largest city, “People make Glasgow”, appears everywhere – on T-shirts, buildings, bus stops and mugs. And when I first moved to Scotland from India in 2018, I was immediately welcomed by kind strangers and helpful neighbours. People showed curiosity, rather than intrusiveness. They respected queues; told me I fit right in. Music, art and cultural events were considered inclusive spaces in the city, with calls for diversity, creativity, inclusion – all the good things.

As an outsider, this was a dream come true: to be myself, to be alone, to have brotherhood and a community. It was life-changing. I could do whatever I wanted, wear whatever I wanted, walk by myself at night, even. That is a luxury, especially for a woman. But something has changed, particularly after Covid, a global recession and years of austerity. Now, I watch the steady rise of far-right, fringe violence and I feel a special scrutiny upon me.

In June, we saw disorder and racists assaults in Glasgow as hundreds of masked protesters marched through the streets. Asian business owners were harassed and people were attacked – according to the police – “because of the colour of their skin”. Later that month, a man was charged with attempted murder after allegedly attacking men leaving a mosque in Edinburgh. A video appeared to show him shouting that he was “protecting the country”. In July, a delivery driver was assaulted after anti-immigration protesters, many of them masked, some shouting racist abuse, once again “rampaged” through Glasgow. We have seen mosques defaced with “hate graffiti” – one is attacked in Britain every five days, according to new data. We’ve heard a speaker at a protest outside an asylum hotel in Falkirk calling for a crowd to “keep Britain white”. There have been activists outside the Scottish parliament staging fascist-style demonstrations. It goes to show top-down propaganda funnels to real-life incidents.

I feel this increasing hostility personally, too. Strangers point-blank question me about my nationality, accent, religion or clothes. A stranger once told me that my accent was weird. An acquaintance said immigrants were taking away jobs from locals, after I told them I was struggling to find work despite being qualified. People jump queues and are quickly confrontational. The “outsiders” that Glasgow loved and accepted have seemingly become the subject of derision and suspicion.

I find people staring at me, head to toe, for an uncomfortably long time. A customer in a Govan pub casually remarked aloud that immigrants are criminals and that we “need to go back”. An old lady on a bus interrupted me and my very white, very British husband to tell us to stop talking the way we were talking. Was it because we’re clearly an interracial couple? Is it because we categorically don’t sound like the locals? I’ll never know, but it’s gnawing now at the back of my mind when it never would have a few short years ago.

Colleagues who have been here since the 1980s and earlier tell me that racist violence has happened in Scotland before, but this time it feels different. We’re afraid to step out now. There’s a clear, marked shift in our levels of nervousness. It is certainly more imminent, more immediate – closer to home.

I blame a combination of factors for this unsettling change: the high cost of living, the worsening climate crisis and the rightwing agenda of some of the mainstream media have all increased resentment and suspicion of one’s neighbours. Then, during the Covid-19 pandemic, many people felt that they had been left alone. That the state wasn’t taking care of them as a democracy is supposed to do.

Even a global health emergency, it seemed, couldn’t make for a better world. Instead of a fairer, more equal or accessible society, we have extreme wealth inequality that is persistent and increasing. And it doesn’t help that inflammatory posts are favoured by social-media algorithms. All of this creates a tinderbox in which people of colour understandably feel afraid.

Many places, including Leith and Glasgow, held anti-racist, pro-immigrant, pro-humanity rallies days after the racist incidents occurred. People carried signs reading: “Racism is weird, have you tried hobbies?”; “Migrants make the NHS”; “Hate has no home”. They made passionate speeches about standing up to bigotry. But is that enough? While it was heartwarming to see thousands of people come out, uniting for diversity, inclusion and multiculturalism, it won’t stop a growing hatred and fear of people like me. And so every time I’m out in public now, my stress levels go up. Am I safe alone? What is my exit strategy? Can I even afford to be angry? Others feel it, too.

I understand why many British people feel overlooked and badly done by – it’s true that Britain is unequal and unfair. But I wish that the media would not validate people’s inherent biases and misconceptions, nor politicians legitimise their worst sentiments by calling for reactions like “pure, cold rage”. It is easy to whip up hatred between neighbours, but systematic hatred and divisiveness can take decades to undo. The only individuals who benefit from scapegoating are the powerful.

We have to say “no” to this normalisation of bigotry, violence and othering. We have to focus on the living conditions and inequality we all share. We need to remember we have more in common with each other than with any billionaire. We must remember that the real blame lies with the system that wants us divided. Talk to real people who look and sound different from you. You’ll realise we’re all humans. We can do better than this.

2026-08-23.title: Why am I called The Black Farmer? Because there are so few of us in Britain. I’d like that to change
2026-08-23.author: Wilfred Emmanuel-Jones
paragraphs: Running a farm is tough – TV’s Clarkson’s Farm shows that – but I know many minorities would love the chance. And we would all benefit

Who’d be a farmer? Clarkson’s Farm on Amazon is great entertainment but it also gives some indication of the stresses and challenges behind the farm gate. Would anyone who lacked the significant alternative income that Clarkson is lucky to have want that? Well, actually, yes.

I’m an entrepreneur who owns a farm, as opposed to hands-on running the small one I bought 25 years ago, but as I look around the industry, I’m struck by a significant fact: the very reason I can be known as the Black Farmer is because I am such a rarity that it makes me readily identifiable.

Because of what I do, people – many of them British minorities – often ask me how they can be farmers, how they can secure some land and set up for themselves. Don’t be surprised at that: among Britain’s minorities, millions have rural origins in lands abroad. It is a mistake to see people of colour as intrinsically urban – my own origins are in rural Jamaica. But when they ask me, I can’t really help them. There is no obvious route for them to follow, and there is precious little land they could possibly farm. This is the reality. In 2025, when Defra completed its most recent survey of principal farmers and holders in England, it found 99.7% of those who responded self-described as white.

I’m aware of the pitfall here. I know the danger these days of wanting to talk about diversity and being dismissed as woke. I’m hardly woke: in 2010 I fought a rural seat for the Conservatives. But in any other industry, that figure, 99.7%, would prompt some questions.

Here are the problems. If you are black or Asian or a kid from another minority in London, or Manchester, or Birmingham or Newcastle, where do you start? Your parents don’t own even an acre of land. You don’t have the network, or the knowledge that comes from growing up within or adjacent to a farming family and a farming community.

There is the ongoing and emotive debate about inheritance tax and whether farms should so easily be passed down from generation to generation. I’m among those who celebrate the families that have worked the same land year after year, decade after decade. That brings a knowledge and continuity essential to rural communities and our food supply. But as well as inheritance, we have to think about entry. People cannot resolve to make that commitment if they cannot see a way in.

How could that be different? Think about who owns the land. The National Trust, for example, is the country’s largest farm-owner, with more than 1,300 tenant farmers. Think about the Duchy of Cornwall, the crown estate, the Church of England. Universities and local authorities also control large tracts of land. There are people and institutions that could administer properly controlled programmes to allow those from non-traditional farming backgrounds to have a go. They could create starter farms and offer affordable tenancies. They could provide mentoring, pairing experienced farmers with ambitious newcomers, and give access to equipment. Maybe there could be targeted apprenticeships, allowing people to learn the ropes on someone else’s farm – a process that may lead to them owning their own farm. One might cite 28-year-old Kaleb Cooper on Clarkson’s farm, although in that case it is clearly the younger man teaching the older how it is done.

The supermarkets could play a role, as they wield enormous influence over British food and how it is produced. Why can’t they create routes for a new generation of growers, providing a sure path for produce to reach the public? That would be a move towards diversity with a clear economic purpose. Farming could do with new blood: people who question the traditions, people who know about different foods, cultures and business models – people who look at a field and can envision things that previous generations couldn’t.

I think back. I grew up in Birmingham and my first experience with the land was helping my father on his allotment. My route was defiantly non-traditional. I struggled with undiagnosed dyslexia, joined the Parachute regiment and got kicked out, flipped burgers, worked as a chef and then produced cookery programmes for the BBC, which allowed me to buy a farm in Devon. Locals dubbed me “the Black Farmer”. I wish there were many more of us.

I would never want to denigrate those who work so hard, and who may have toiled for generations to run their farms, produce the food we need and sometimes – if they are lucky, if the weather permits, if the stars align – make a profit. But I also want to be just as excited by the prospect of another black kid from Birmingham getting an opportunity, or a minority kid from a council estate in Manchester becoming the first farmer in the family.
Farming is key to the future, and the climate crisis is forcing us to think fast and hard about crops, water, soil and what we do with them. Old timers, new thinkers – we need both.

2026-08-23.title: It’s Harry and Meghan in Finding Freedom 2: Back in Blighty
2026-08-23.author: Marina Hyde
paragraphs: Hard to fathom exactly why Megxit is over and the self-exiled wonder generators are leaving California. Luckily, the internet sleuths are on the case

Wednesday night brought an absolute cloudburst of psychic rain for our parched land, as it emerged that Prince Harry and Meghan were reversing their self-styled “freedom flight” to California and returning to live in the UK. Nature is healing! Is that … is that how the expression goes? Either way, all humans in Britain have taken the announcement brilliantly, while fatted calf prices climbed steeply at the news that the reverse Megxit is imminent, with only an adequate headline soubriquet yet to be found. Megain? Megraine?

Inevitably, thoughts turned swiftly to what it all meant. One of the funniest aspects of Meghan and Harry coverage is how their decisions are always analysed as though we were parsing the 4D chess moves of 19th-century master strategists. We are forever imagining we are dealing with a couple of Bismarcks or Clausewitzes, as opposed to a resting actor and the “chief impact officer” of a firm designed to offer tech-based solutions to men crying in their cars or something.

And so it is that motive is being obsessively pored over. There’s definitely some eye-catching speculation out there. Some feel that Meghan being willing to step so much as a toe on to our toxic shores can only be a way of telegraphing the unfortunate suggestion that the king’s days are numbered. Or maybe Harry just wants to spend more time with his £9.5m legal bill. Others have spicier takes. I saw a few horrified Sussex Squad Americans on social media suggesting that the only conceivable explanation is that Prince Harry is simply a world-beating god of sex. Allow me to expand. I’m sure the squad diehards won’t mind me projecting their own psychological projections on to Meghan, but the logic seemed comparable to someone saying: “Sorry, so the suggestion is that I move back to live on top of a live volcano, in a plague-ridden failed state, run by psychopathically violent warlords. Who’s asking?” 1990s-era Keanu Reeves. “BRB just calling the removal firm.”

Multiple other takes are of course available. In Hong Kong, they used to have an acronym for bankers who were too stupid to get the good jobs in London but were able to move out there and do very nicely: Filth (Failed in London, try Hong Kong). It’s not as good, acronym-wise, but I guess we could be looking at a Fimuk situation – Failed in Montecito, try UK. No doubt we’ve all forgotten the full ins and outs, but I believe Ellen DeGeneres has been on a similar journey. It’s possible that the Sussexes have just failed to keep pace with the elite fruit-spread makers of California, and that Meghan believes the waters of home counties jam-making will be much less competitive. I look forward to her conveying this judgment to the local Women’s Institute at her earliest convenience.
Or, look, possibly the real reason for this move is something in between all these things – but which of us wants to be wasting time on nuance right now?

What we do know is that it’s definitely on, and the couple’s children are enrolled in a school for September. Early thoughts? Mainly that someone’s class WhatsApp group just got an incredible new member. Speaking as a veteran of these digital abysses of passive aggression, may I state that the absolute last thing you need on one is someone whose stated life philosophy is to “create wonder in every moment”.

Seriously. You simply cannot run the risk of the following message materialising at Christmas/in high summer when you are limping towards the holidays. “Thinking about end-of-term presents, I thought it would be really magical to create a mirror where the frame is our children’s handprints. I can organise?” Really? Because I’ve been hurt before. But go on. “Literally all I would need from you ladies is a clay cast of your daughter’s hand with a pressed daisy picked by moonlight embedded in it. If anyone hasn’t pressed flowers before I would be very happy to offer a (fun!) tutorial at my place on Tuesday after drop-off.” Aaaaaaaaaaaagh. Please, I HAVE A JOB. I CAN’T DO ANY OF THIS. You know what everyone loves? John Lewis vouchers. Please. PLEASE. As for other events during the school year, might as well call the Vatican right now because I can assure you we have a nailed-on bake sale martyr on our hands right here.

Still, this is all very sad news for the country of the United States of America, and its now decimated entertainment industry, as Harry and Meghan leave behind them failed deals with Spotify and Netflix, among others. Then again, have they? Recent years have seen the Sussexes hamstrung by having exhaustively told the only story of theirs that anyone is remotely interested in. I can hardly believe I’m typing this, but it turned out no one wants to watch documentaries about global justice activism or polo. But this week’s news could easily reignite the only kind of content Netflix’s degraded first-look deal with Meghan would be extremely interested in having a first look at: the one where their life is made miserable by a toxic family in a toxic country with a toxic press. And then you make TV all about it.

It’s a bit like when there’s been a hugely successful movie with a crazy, high-concept situation, and the producers of the sequel just have to work out a way to get the characters back into the same crazy, high-concept situation, or at least a similar one, so they can go back to the money well for a second time. Having been on board a bus that can’t slow down, Speed 2 finds Sandra Bullock on a runaway cruise ship. Home Alone 2 sees Kevin once again left behind, this time in New York as opposed to Chicago, where the same burglars have somehow rematerialised. In Finding Freedom 2, it’ll probably work best for the Sussexes to embrace the absurdity with a cheeky one-liner. When Harry and Meghan are battling remorseless tabloid attention, poisonous family dynamics, and deranged public antipathy, let’s hope he turns to the Netflix cameras and quotes Bruce Willis in Die Hard 2: “How can the same shit happen to the same guy twice?” I don’t know, mate – but I assume you’re getting first-dollar gross on the box office.

In the meantime, the shock news continues to spark an hourly carousel of #onlyinBritain questions. What’s going to happen on Remembrance Sunday? Will this mean “rival courts”? Hand on heart, it’s hard to escape the conclusion that there are, amazingly, a whole lot of people who are even more ridiculous and even more emotional than Harry and Meghan. And – also amazingly – they are not the population of the state of California.

2026-08-23.title: Nigel Farage called us ‘nobodies’ in the Clacton byelection. He seems to treat the town in much the same way
2026-08-23.author: Attieh Fard
paragraphs: I had few resources as a candidate, but the contest allowed me to speak to local people about their lives and their MP. They deserve so much better

In the early hours of last Friday morning, a video was posted. It showed Nigel Farage among his team of volunteers, before the votes had been counted, celebrating his victory and saying that he was not going to humiliate himself by sharing a platform at the count next to “nobodies”.

He was referring to the 33 other candidates who had taken part in what was effectively an unnecessary election, one Farage himself had instigated just a few weeks earlier to send one message: that the people of Clacton were backing him, despite parliamentary investigations into his receipt of an undeclared £5m donation. The election is over, but it’s worth thinking about Clacton and those candidates, of whom I was one.

I migrated to Britain from Iran 27 years ago, and have not been back there for 24 years because my Christian faith and my political activities put me at risk of persecution. Iran’s Islamic regime has massacred thousands of innocent people who want the democracy and freedom we have in Britain and it continues to execute protesters. Perhaps that’s why I felt so passionately about defending our democratic system in Britain from being abused.

Some in the British-Iranian community had high respect for Farage as it was not long ago that he met and embraced protesters outside the Iranian embassy in London after the Islamic regime’s massacres. Many of them were puzzled as to why I was standing against him and why I had left the Conservatives, for whom I had previously stood as a candidate in local elections, to do so. I remember Reform supporters in Surrey asking me: if Farage could not save the country, who could? My decision to stand was not a personal vendetta however. Having closely followed Reform’s campaigns on immigration, borders and security, I had seen the deep divides they created in communities.

Throughout the election, Farage did his best to keep his distance from the other candidates. He refused to engage with us, to attend hustings and ultimately to share a platform on the night of the count.

The campaign itself was revealing, as I met voters who had become disillusioned with Farage. Some were frustrated that he had never visited them or replied to their constituency emails. Others were concerned about his undeclared multimillion pound funds and connections with crypto billionaires. Some felt he had done almost nothing for Clacton, or that he had put Clacton “on the map for the wrong reasons”. Others were angry that he had triggered a byelection, wasting about £250,000 of taxpayers’ money.
Interestingly, some who had previously voted for Reform because they were concerned about immigration changed their minds when they learned more.

As an expert in immigration law, I was able to explain why the small boat crossings were happening. Leaving the EU meant that the UK was no longer part of the Dublin III regulation and could therefore no longer return asylum seekers to the first safe country in which they had arrived. When the UK left the EU, it created a legal void in relation to returning asylum seekers to EU countries.

They also learned how some of our laws do not make sense. An asylum seeker has to be physically present in the UK before making a claim, rather than being able to make a claim from overseas and have their identity and background checked before arrival.
Did they know that Farage had criticised the Rwanda scheme as a “con”? No. Did they know that he said it was “a political impossibility” to deport all illegal migrants? No.

Were they aware that he was planning to take the UK out of the Refugee Convention, which allows those being persecuted by regimes such as those in North Korea and Iran to seek protection in another country? No. Did they agree with protecting genuine asylum seekers? Yes.

Did they know that leaving the European convention on human rights without replacing it with a British bill of rights could affect British citizens and their rights relating to privacy and freedom of expression? No.

Having only two weeks to knock on doors, and a few hours each day on my feet to talk to those who were willing to listen was hard, but 126 residents backed my campaign. I have since received messages of support from some of them, telling me that if I stand again, they would help. I am honoured.

One fact became clear. People want the Clacton MP to tackle crime in his constituency, to address its infrastructure weaknesses, and to create more opportunities for its young people and families. Farage isn’t doing any of these things, so how likely is it that he can renew Britain?
Given all these issues, it was unsurprising that so much of the electorate did not support him. He won, but Nigel Farage MP has some serious work to do in Clacton.

2026-08-24.title: Walking the Peak District, I discovered a wonderful rejection of the right’s monotone vision of England
2026-08-24.author: John Harris
paragraphs: The landscape was striking, but so was the diversity of the hikers. We can make this the new normal – and we should

A fortnight or so ago, my two teenage kids and I set out on a three-night visit to the Peak District where temperatures were hovering at a comparatively tepid 28C. We stayed at a youth hostel – more of which in a moment – and began the trip with the 20-minute ascent of Mam Tor, a modest peak that pulls in both dedicated ramblers who then yomp along the ridge beyond, and newbies who mostly want to get to the top and immerse themselves in the jaw-dropping view.

The next bit might sound self-parodically Guardian-esque, but what the hell: in its own way, the most striking sight was the diversity of the scores of people rambling up, down and along. Women in their 20s wearing hijabs picnicked on giant rocks, while multiracial gaggles of young men attempted to race to the top; solo and shirtless white fitness freaks and retirement-age dog walkers took their places alongside them. With plenty of justification, country walking has long been typified as one of the most monoculturally white pursuits there is. But here – presumably because of the relatively close proximity of Manchester and Sheffield – things looked different.

The scenes didn’t quite suggest Britain in microcosm, but they weren’t far off. I began to wonder, in fact, whether I was witnessing the (extremely) belated next emancipatory phase of a story that began with the mass trespass at the nearby Kinder Scout in 1932, led by the Jewish anti-fascist Benny Rothman: the protest in which hundreds of men and women defied the law to walk on privately owned Derbyshire hills and moorland. Five of them received prison sentences, but the way was thereby opened to the creation of the UK’s first national parks.

The latter-day people and organisations working to make walking more inclusive – in response to national statistics that remain depressing, and often in the face of straight-up prejudice – surely deserve as much praise as Rothman and his comrades. Black Girls Hike was founded in 2019 by the brilliant Mancunian Rhiane Fatinikun, aimed at creating “a safe space for Black women to explore the outdoors … challenging the status quo”. Soon after, the Coventry-based rambler Haroon Mota started Muslim Hikers, and began group walks just over a year later. In the same city, Cherelle Harding created Steppers UK, intended to “normalise black and brown faces in outdoor spaces and create a community of outdoor enthusiasts”.

All this reflects aspects of our culture and politics that can be fascinating and inspiring – and, on the other side of some modern political and cultural divides, very unsettling. If he were to visit the Peak District, Nigel Farage would presumably get no further than his chosen pub. But his vision of bucolic England is symbolised by the outfit he tends to wear when he wants to accuse the supposed metropolitan elite of neglecting the countryside, usually by turning up at one of those faux – or not so faux – fox hunts. We all know the drill: flat cap, Barbour jacket, wellies, fag and pint. The cosplay is replete with meaning, and not just in its embodiment of what a cultural-studies specialist might call white rurality. Look, for example, at the terrible twist Farage and his political allies got their collective knickers in over the National Trust’s drive to be open about some of its properties’ links to colonialism and slavery, and the same organisation’s campaigning to protect the environment.

Further to the right, somewhere in the heart of every nativist lurk darkly romanticised visions of the British landscape – think of what is meant by that toxic phrase “blood and soil”. Last year, news broke about two wooded stretches of land in mid-Wales being bought by the Woodlander Initiative, a scheme led by the far-right activist Simon Birkett. He has links to Patriotic Alternative, reckoned to be the UK’s largest fascist organisation. The people involved were never going to be interested in urban land: to the fascist mind, the countryside, as opposed to the cosmopolitan and decadent stereotypical city (think about the far right’s constant demonisation of London), represents notions of racial purity and noble simplicity. From some far-right activists, there was sympathetic talk in response about “indigenous heartlands – places for our people”.

The upshot of all this is obvious: the UK’s rural expanses can be as toxified and contested as any other aspect of our national life, and without wanting to sound too dour – walking is meant to be fun, after all – we need to actively promote the idea that the countryside belongs to all of us. To do so is to deprive the assortment of opportunists and hate-mongers who span the hard and far right of any idea that the British landscape and its romance and mythology might be theirs to monopolise.

There is another, much more benign and everyday obstacle to maximising access to green spaces. In many places, hotels and hospitality increasingly embody a different kind of exclusivity: the upgrading of pubs and hotels to boutique, gastro-centric establishments with sky-high prices. Those charged on such platforms as Airbnb are part of the same problem. So if your ambitions extend further than a day trip and such luxury is beyond your budget, where can you stay?

Part of the answer lies with the Youth Hostels Association (YHA) of England and Wales (the equivalent north of the border is Hostelling Scotland) and its network of places to eat, sleep and socialise. But the pandemic caused the YHA an income loss of £40m in the first year alone, and in March last year, it said that its energy costs had quadrupled. In 2023, it had about 150 hostels; to date, it has announced the sale or closure of 29. Eight are now run as hostels thanks to a YHA franchising scheme, and there are similar hopes for at least one of my threatened favourites: Bellever on Dartmoor, one of the most idyllic places I have ever spent the night.

But here is the crucial point: the YHA runs a programme that provides fully or “partly funded stays at youth hostels for young people and families facing significant challenges” (including young carers, and those involved in refugee and migrant groups), and a scheme called No Child Left Behind that helps to ensure that financial hardship does not stop kids going on residential school trips. It is an organisation that should be expanding, not shrinking.

Having come down off Mam Tor, I drove the half hour back to where we were staying: Hartington Hall, a 17th-century manor house owned and run by the YHA. As we were having dinner, I noticed a plaque fixed to the wall, presumably dating from the distant days (the YHA was founded in 1930) when guests were obliged to muck in with the chores rather than sample the £14 burger-and-beer meal deal. “This youth hostel,” it said, “is one of many, both in this country and abroad, where young people, regardless of race or creed, may spend the night. The buildings are diverse in character but they have a common purpose: to help all, especially young people of limited means, to a greater knowledge, love and care for the countryside.”

How, then, to preserve as many hostels as possible, bring in more young people and make those words real? An injection of cash from big-spending philanthropists? A modest tourist tax on hotels and short-let accommodation? Or the kind of relative loose change that could presumably be found by the departments for Food and Rural Affairs, Education, Culture, Media and Sport, or all three? Some parts of the British landscape are starting to undergo what seems to be an overdue and very welcome social change, but it needs the kind of support that comes in the form of bunk-beds and brickwork. In a country whose divisions are constantly inflamed and hyped up by demagogic chancers, that challenge is a lot more urgent than it might seem.

2026-08-24.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s foreign policy: work in progress
2026-08-24.author: Editorial
paragraphs: The prime minister has focused on domestic affairs since coming to office. But at a time of global disruption, he will need to define Britain’s place in the world

A run of volatility in domestic British politics in recent years has tracked a period of global turbulence, and yet foreign policy over the same period has been an area of relative stability. What little is known about Andy Burnham’s approach to international relations expresses more continuity with Sir Keir Starmer’s administration than deviation. In negotiations with the EU, the red lines that prohibit membership of the single market or customs union still stand. Where Washington is concerned, Mr Burnham shows no interest in performances of bonhomie with Donald Trump, but his predecessor had already swapped that approach for a cooler pragmatic tone by the end of his tenure.

The new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has opened a good dialogue with Marco Rubio, his US counterpart. Such is the density of integration in defence and security matters that incoming UK prime ministers, regardless of ideology, have little choice but to invest time in cultivating a bond with whoever sits in the White House. Anyone hoping for a spectacular transatlantic rupture and sudden clinch with Brussels will be disappointed.

Some patterns of consistency date back beyond the recent transfer of power within the Labour party to the previous Conservative administrations. Support for Ukraine in the face of Russian aggression was one of the few creditable positions taken by Boris Johnson, and that line has held through four transfers of power in Downing Street.

The process of rebuilding functional relations with European neighbours predated the 2024 general election. Rishi Sunak negotiated the Windsor framework for Northern Ireland. He also ditched a bill that threatened chaos for businesses by vaporising retained EU laws without a timetable to replace them.

The business secretary who executed that U-turn in defiance of the Tories’ fanatical Eurosceptic tendency was Kemi Badenoch. It was not a choice she highlighted in her subsequent bid to become Conservative leader. By then the party, relieved of the burden of governing responsibility, was in no mood to consider the merits of pragmatism where Europe was concerned.

Having withdrawn to an ideological comfort zone, the Tories still cannot pretend that Brexit has been a success. Sir Keir became gradually more confident in attributing Britain’s economic woes to the terms of departure from the EU. But the shift was largely rhetorical because he was locked into a manifesto commitment that precluded a substantial change of direction. Mr Burnham has accepted the same constraint as a condition of his hand-me-down electoral mandate.

Having accepted the parameters of Boris Johnson’s hard Brexit and acknowledged Britain’s security dependency on Washington, the prime minister doesn’t have much room to innovate in foreign policy. Nor has he shown much interest, focusing instead on domestic issues that are much more salient to voters than geopolitics.

That is a rational priority for a new leader hoping to win over sceptical voters. But with no sign of global volatility abating, an international crisis will force itself on to Mr Burnham’s agenda soon enough. Global strife, especially when it whips up economic headwinds, quickly manifests itself as pressure to act in domestic politics. The prime minister has proved adept at connecting with an audience close to home. That advantage will be degraded if he cannot also connect his domestic agenda to a coherent strategy for engagement with the wider world.

2026-08-24.title: The Guardian view on the new Hungary: de-Orbánising at pace
2026-08-24.author: Editorial
paragraphs: As a Brussels deadline looms with over €10bn at stake, Péter Magyar’s first three months have been transformative in addressing a corrupt legacy

Some elections are more important than others. Since taking office in May, Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, has embarked upon the country’s most far-reaching and dramatic programme of transformation since the fall of communism in 1989. Mr Magyar’s predecessor, Viktor Orbán, established a soft autocracy which thrived on corruption and, over 16 years, exerted its grip on most areas of Hungarian life, from religion to culture and the media. It is being dismantled at extraordinary pace.

Last week, a newly appointed president took office following the sacking of Tamás Sulyok, accused by Mr Magyar of having rubber-stamped the erosion of the rule of law in the country. In stark contrast, András Baka is a former president of Hungary’s supreme court, a role he was removed from by the Orbán regime in an action judged unlawful by the European court of human rights.

On Hungary’s national day last Thursday, news bulletins returned to the main state television channel, having been shut down for six weeks. In July, viewers had encountered a blank screen along with the message: “Public media should not lie. We are sorry for doing it for so long.” Ending naked bias on state TV was one of Mr Magyar’s key pledges, in a campaign that saw him buck an electoral system weighted in favour of Mr Orbán and win a landslide.

The tempo has been equally relentless when it comes to attacking networks of corruption and clientelism built up over a decade and a half. Well over €100bn in public funds, including billions of euros of EU money, is believed to have been siphoned off during the Orbán years. Investigators have been empowered to go after it via a new National Asset Recovery and Protection Office. Mr Magyar has also confirmed Hungarian participation in the European public prosecutor’s office, enabling the EU to better protect itself from financial crime in the country.

It will take time for Hungary to feel like a normal pluralist European democracy again. For now, Mr Magyar is functioning as a one-man political whirlwind, heading what amounts to a national unity government elected by voters across the political spectrum. Concerns have been raised over constitutional manoeuvring to ensure many MPs in Mr Orbán’s Fidesz party cannot stand again, and Mr Baka has warned against appearing to take revenge on the former prime minister’s supporters. But a root-and-branch approach to de-Orbánising Hungary was what was needed, and continues to be rewarded by record levels of popularity in polls.

The next major threshold is likely to be crossed in the autumn. Brussels has given Hungary’s new government until the end of this month to demonstrate that enough is being done on corruption to warrant the release of over €10bn in frozen funds. If, as seems likely, the vast majority of the funds are disbursed, it will seal the ongoing rapprochement between the EU and its former rogue member state.

In May, Mr Magyar relocated the prime minister’s office away from a controversially cordoned-off former Carmelite monastery used by Mr Orbán, opening the building up to the public. “I was not elected simply to change the government, but to change the regime,” he had told interviewers soon after taking power. Three months on, the symbolism is being supplemented by a peaceful political revolution.

2026-08-24.title: To end homelessness, look to the root causes
2026-08-24.author: Letters
paragraphs: Readers respond to Andy Burnham’s pledge to get all rough sleepers off the streets by Christmas

As a vulnerable teenage girl carrying my life in a rucksack, I have been the person Andy Burnham describes people walking past in his article (I won’t abandon anyone to sleep rough on our streets. That’s my £442m promise, 19 August). That experience taught me that homelessness is far more complex than rough sleeping alone, and that ending it takes more than getting people off the streets.

Getting everyone in for Christmas is an important ambition. But lasting success means preventing people from reaching crisis point and giving those who do the practical support and opportunities they need. I was lucky. Public sector work gave me structure, stability, and someone willing to believe in my potential.
Housing must sit alongside education, healthcare, employment and social mobility, giving people not just somewhere to live, but a genuine route to stability, independence and opportunity.

This is why charities and initiatives such as Homewards, with a collaborative, prevention-first approach, are so important. Solving homelessness takes joined-up support, earlier intervention, and a belief that people need routes into housing, work, health, safety and belonging. As Mr Burnham rightly says, homelessness is a problem to solve, not step around. Prevention must be at the heart of that solution.Dr Sabrina Cohen-HattonChief fire officer, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service

The prime minister’s pledge to end rough sleeping is admirable, and he’s right about the importance of catching people “long before they hit the pavement”. But to succeed, the he must confront the Home Office’s role in creating homelessness. Last year, around 21,000 households in England needed homelessness help after eviction from Home Office accommodation.

Research by the Refugee Council and others has highlighted how delayed documentation, inadequate support and too little time to find accommodation leave refugees facing homelessness and destitution within weeks of a being given leave to stay in the UK.

Current plans making refugee status more precarious, putting refugees in thousands of pounds of debt and further restricting asylum support will only worsen this. Until the Home Office stops pushing refugees on to the streets, ending rough sleeping will be out of reach.Imran HussainRefugee Council

As a psychiatrist, I have seen an increasing number of patients with severe mental health difficulties ending up homeless, and the local council concluding that it doesn’t have a duty to house them as they have made themselves “intentionally homeless” by failing to stick to the rules.

This is usually because the patient has used drugs on the premises and they are evicted from their temporary accommodation. They are then expected to demonstrate three months of abstinence while being street homeless before they can try again for accommodation – with no understanding that housing will aid their ability to get off drugs.

While I have some sympathy for the local authority’s position, we need to have a system that thinks housing first, with recognition the reducing drug use takes time and requires wraparound support from mental health and drug services.

Until that happens, I fear Andy Burnham’s new initiative will result in accommodation being found, but the patient quickly falling foul of the rules, and the local authorities washing their hands of them again.Dr Charles DixonExeter

2026-08-24.title: Is this why close encounters with intelligent aliens have so far eluded us?
2026-08-24.author: Letters
paragraphs: Readers offer their explanations for the absence of hard evidence for extraterrestrial civilisations, in response to an article by Adam Kirsch

When thinking about why we have not encountered intelligent aliens yet, as Adam Kirsch does (The long read, 11 August), it seems to me that one factor gets neglected: fossil fuels. Alien life could develop intelligence on myriad planets, but to develop advanced technology that would enable them to get off‑world, they need to go through an equivalent of the Industrial Revolution, and that needed first coal, then oil and gas.
There could be many intelligent alien races out there, but on planets without an easily accessible fossil fuel equivalent, they’d never get past a 17th-century level of development.

Even if we can eventually detect life on planets outside our solar system, we’d never know these civilisations existed, as their signature from afar would be indistinguishable from that of a planet with just plant-like life and a fire ecology.

It is entirely probable, as a result, that almost all alien races, if they exist, are living in an eternal equivalent of Game of Thrones’s Westeros, not Iain M Banks’s Culture, doomed never to be detected from afar.Ian SimmonsWestcliff-on-Sea, Essex

Adam Kirsch’s article misses one possibility: that any advanced civilisation might simply be keeping its distance. Humans have long imagined such watchers. The Kayapó people of Brazil, for example, tell of Bep Kororoti, a visitor who shared knowledge and helped their ancestors build a stable and sustainable society.

It’s easy to imagine a similar conversation among distant observers today. A younger voice might look at our atomic weapons and shake its head, predicting that we’ll finish ourselves off. An older voice might reply that humans have a habit of rebuilding, and that societies like the Kayapó show we can live with balance when we choose. Their verdict might be to wait a while, and see whether we can keep our civilisation going, before attempting contact. Given our history, who could blame them?Miland JoshiBirmingham

Given the age of the universe, estimated at 13.8bn years, it is quite possible that many forms of life and civilisations have arisen, flourished, declined and disappeared (just as humanity seems likely to). The notion that two such phenomena might occur at the same time and thus permit mutual communication would be a mind-boggling cosmic coincidence. So one response to Fermi’s question “Where is everybody?” might be “they all left before we got here” or “they haven’t arrived yet, and we’ll be gone by the time they do”.David WalkerSheffield
Maybe aliens have arrived, but were too small for us to notice? Perhaps they fell down a drain, were eaten by seagulls, or ended up in an ants’ nest?Sheila PrestonShoreham-by-Sea, West Sussex

2026-08-25.title: The Great Dictator by Matthew Sweet review – the life of Barbara Cartland
2026-08-25.author: Kathryn Hughes
paragraphs: An excellent, compassionate biography of the wildly prolific romantic novelist

Barbara Cartland was famous for dictating her novels. With a pekingese clamped to her hot pink bosom she would lie back on a library couch and exhale a story about virginal girls taming wayward dukes, damaged airmen or misunderstood surgeons. Meanwhile Miss Savory, Mrs Smith or Mrs Morgan, picked for being unfidgety and sneezeless, would take everything down in immaculate Pitman shorthand. Cartland reckoned on being able to polish off 8,000 words a day. “In this way,” she told one of the many reporters who quizzed her on her astonishing productivity, “the typescript for an 80,000-word novel is finished in a fortnight.” At her peak she was pushing out 23 books a year which added up to 723 in total. Only Agatha Christie and William Shakespeare topped her lifetime sales of 750m.

Cartland was a dictator in other ways, too. Husbands, dogs, houses and the local council were all expected to bend themselves to her indomitable will. Resistance, let alone opposition, was futile. The managing director of the company that printed her books suggested that she read Nietzsche on the perceptive grounds that they had a lot of ideas in common. Oddly, he also declared himself madly in love with her. Behind that marshmallowy exterior, all pink chiffon, candyfloss hair and soft, smudgy lines, there lurked sinews of high-tensile steel.

Anyone expecting this biography of Barbara Cartland to be an amusing takedown of a monstre sacré along the lines of Craig Brown’s witty 2017 decimation of Princess Margaret will be disappointed. Rather, Matthew Sweet pays his subject the compliment of absolute seriousness, regarding her as a cultural phenomenon whose extraordinary life, stretching the entire 20th century, deserves deep study. Sweet has had unfettered access to the cornucopia of material that Cartland left behind at Camfield Place, the Hertfordshire manor house where she lived until her death in 2000 at the age of 98. Conducting a fingertip search of her letters, scrapbooks and typescripts, Sweet has crafted a generous but clear-sighted account of a woman who was too often reduced to the status of a lazy joke.

She was born in 1901 into the lower upper class. On her father’s side she was pure trade. James Cartland and Son was a Birmingham metalworkers turning out umbrella stands, crocodile-shaped inkwells, shelf brackets shaped like sea monsters and “pharaonic letterboxes embossed with meaningless hieroglyphs”. Her adored mother Polly, meanwhile, was Gloucestershire gentry and there had been the usual rows about marrying down. Cartland’s paternal grandfather killed himself when the business went bust and her father retreated into alcoholism, leaving Polly to manage the tricky business of getting her daughter launched into a life the family could no longer afford.

Sweet suggests that this constellation of losses and compensations set the emotional template for Cartland’s adult life. Men were necessary but fragile and certainly best not relied upon. Having come out as a deb in 1919 into a world where there were not enough husbands to go round, Barbara set out to become financially self-sufficient by plunging into the only kind of work for which she was qualified. For the next decade she filed gossipy titbits about young London society to the Express, the Mirror and the Daily Mail.

This was the world of the Bright Young Things, so often written up today as a madcap time of pyjama parties and midnight dashes to the continent. In fact, Cartland’s columns reveal a society still in shock from the first world war: fathers are dead (Cartland lost hers in the trenches in 1918), grand family houses have been sold, divorce is everywhere and life seems impossible without alcohol or drugs. The men whom Cartland stepped out with were not the heart-throb dukes and dashing airmen that she would later write about, but broken people without the language to express their desolation. “My contemporaries were ashamed to show emotion,” she observed with characteristic perception in her 1943 memoir The Isthmus Years. “We had all of us a horror of sympathy.”

So instead she simply carried on with a brittle determination to make the best of things. After plenty of dalliances with men called things like Pingo Langrishe and Nigs Ratendone she made a tactical marriage to a dull man called Alexander McCorquodale who was heir to a printing fortune. When he retreated into drink – shades of her father – she effected a neat swap by divorcing, then marrying his paternal cousin. In this way there was no need to change her surname: she had replaced one Mr McCorquodale with another. It rankled that she never achieved a title until she herself was made a Dame in 1991. By contrast, her ambitious daughter, Raine, managed to insert herself into the peerage not once but three times through each of her carefully strategic marriages.

The only man who really mattered to Cartland was her beloved younger brother, Ronald. They went on holiday together and endlessly discussed the cod-eastern philosophies that were all the rage in the 1920s: Ouspensky and Gurdjieff were favourites and Cartland retained a vague mysticism to the end of her life involving ghosts and spiritual healing. She also believed in flying saucers and the power of honey to cure just about anything.

Brother and sister bonded too over politics, specifically a socially engaged, internationalist Toryism. Barbara bossed Ronald into parliament where he became a leading anti-appeaser. She in turn wrote one of the first of the tiny number of 1930s British novels that dealt specifically with the evils of Nazi antisemitism. Dangerous Experiment (1936) involves the improbable story of Lena Carrington who, after a shipwreck and a spell as the slave of a tribe of thunder-worshippers in the Caucasus, ends up in Germany where she is courted by a Nazi lover. In the end she breaks things off when she sees him mistreating a Jewish refugee.

This, of course, is not the Barbara Cartland that most of us remember from the 80s and beyond. In what Sweet calls her “imperial phase” she was writing novels with paper-thin plots that she endlessly recycled. She was also a relentless self-promoter. Bed linen, candles and towels were all enthusiastically marketed under her name, although with remarkable restraint she drew the line at scented toilet paper. She also pulled off a promotion with Dewhurst the butcher, which offered customers one of six previously unpublished Cartland novels for every £12 they spent. The promotion was not a great success because of the sheer weirdness of “being given a copy of Desire in the Desert with a parcel of mince”.

But when, in a stroke of fortune so improbable that even now it hardly seems real, her daughter, Raine, became Diana Spencer’s stepmother, Cartland sensed new opportunities for cross-pollination. She took to announcing “I invented virgins” and managed to imply that the royal wedding of 1981 was somehow her doing, despite being pointedly not invited. Raine, a chip off the old block, made sure that the gift shop at the Spencer family seat, Althorp, stocked a full run of Barbara Cartlands.

It would be easy to dismiss Cartland as a quirk, an aberration the likes of which we will not see again. But the great triumph of this brilliant book is the way that Sweet embeds her firmly in the economic, political, social and artistic transformations of the 20th century while charting the ways in which she also transcended them. Somehow, and this remains the deep mystery of it all, Barbara Cartland emerges as that rather admirable thing: an entirely self-made woman.
2026-08-25.titleKo: 매튜 스위트의 『위대한 구술자』 서평 – 바버라 카틀랜드의 삶
2026-08-25.standfirstKo: 경이로운 다작으로 유명한 로맨스 소설가의 삶을 깊고 따뜻한 시선으로 조명한 탁월한 평전
paragraphsKo: 경이로운 다작을 남긴 로맨스 소설가 바버라 카틀랜드의 삶을 깊고 따뜻한 시선으로 조명한 탁월한 평전이다.

바버라 카틀랜드는 소설을 '구술(dictating)'하여 집필하는 것으로 유명했다. 핫핑크빛 가슴팍에 페키니즈 강아지를 꼭 껴안은 채 서재 소파에 기대어 누워, 순결한 처녀들이 제멋대로인 공작이나 상처 입은 비행사, 혹은 오해받는 외과의사를 길들이는 이야기를 거침없이 토해내곤 했다. 그동안 안절부절못하거나 재채기를 하지 않는다는 이유로 엄선된 세이보리 양이나 스미스 부인, 모건 부인이 흠잡을 데 없는 피트먼 속기법으로 그 모든 말을 빠짐없이 받아적었다. 카틀랜드는 하루에 8,000단어를 거뜬히 해치울 수 있다고 자신했다. 그녀의 경이로운 생산성에 대해 꼬치꼬치 묻는 수많은 기자 중 한 명에게 그녀는 이렇게 말했다. '이런 방식으로 작업하면 8만 단어 분량의 장편소설 원고가 단 2주 만에 완성된답니다.' 전성기 시절 그녀는 1년에 23권의 책을 쏟아냈으며, 평생 총 723권을 출간했다. 7억 5천만 권에 달하는 그녀의 생애 누적 판매 부수를 넘어선 이는 애거서 크리스티와 윌리엄 셰익스피어뿐이었다.

카틀랜드는 다른 면에서도 한 명의 '독재자(dictator)'였다. 남편, 반려견, 가옥, 심지어 지역 의회조차도 그녀의 꺾이지 않는 완강한 의지에 굴복해야 했다. 반발은커녕 소극적인 저항조차 무의미했다. 그녀의 책을 인쇄하던 출판사 대표는 그녀와 니체가 많은 생각을 공유하고 있다는 날카로운 통찰을 근거로 니체를 읽어보라고 권하기도 했다. 기묘하게도 그는 자신이 그녀에게 미친 듯이 반했다고 고백하기도 했다. 온통 핑크빛 시폰과 솜사탕 같은 머리카락, 부드럽고 몽환적인 화장으로 뒤덮인 마시멜로 같은 외양 뒤편에는 초고장력 강철로 엮인 질긴 근육이 숨어 있었다.

바버라 카틀랜드의 이번 평전이 2017년 크레이그 브라운이 마거릿 공주를 재치 있게 난도질했던 것처럼, '신성불가침의 괴물'을 재미나게 깎아내리는 폭로극일 것이라 기대하는 이가 있다면 실망할 것이다. 오히려 매튜 스위트는 20세기 전체를 관통한 그녀의 비범한 삶이 깊이 있는 연구 대상이라는 판단 아래, 그녀를 하나의 거대한 문화적 현상으로 바라보며 철저하게 진지한 존중을 표한다. 스위트는 카틀랜드가 2000년 98세의 나이로 세상을 떠날 때까지 살았던 하트퍼드셔의 저택 캠필드 플레이스에 남겨진 방대한 자료에 무제한으로 접근할 수 있었다. 그녀의 편지와 스크랩북, 타자 원고를 샅샅이 뒤진 끝에, 스위트는 너무나 오랫동안 손쉬운 조롱거리로 격하되곤 했던 한 여성의 삶을 관대하면서도 명료한 시선으로 복원해 냈다.

그녀는 1901년 하층 상류계급(lower upper class) 가문에서 태어났다. 부친 쪽은 순수한 상업 계통이었다. '제임스 카틀랜드 앤 선'은 우산꽂이, 악어 모양 잉크병, 바다괴물 형상의 선반 받침대, 그리고 '무의미한 상형문자가 양각된 파라오풍 우편함'을 제작하던 버밍엄의 금속 제조업체였다. 반면 그녀가 열렬히 사모했던 어머니 폴리는 글로스터셔의 유서 깊은 젠트리 계급 출신이었기에, 격이 떨어지는 가문과의 결혼을 둘러싼 집안의 불화가 끊이지 않았다. 사업이 파산하자 친조부는 스스로 목숨을 끊었고 아버지는 알코올 중독에 빠져버렸으며, 결국 가족이 더 이상 감당할 수 없게 된 화려한 사교계로 딸을 데뷔시키는 험난한 과제는 오롯이 어머니 폴리의 몫으로 남겨졌다.

스위트는 이러한 상실과 보상의 결합이 카틀랜드의 성인기 삶을 지배하는 정서적 틀을 형성했다고 분석한다. 남성은 반드시 필요하지만 깨지기 쉬운 존재이며, 결코 전적으로 기댈 대상이 아니었다. 남편감이 턱없이 부족했던 제1차 세계대전 직후인 1919년 사교계 데뷔탕트로 첫발을 내딛은 바버라는, 자신이 자격을 갖춘 유일한 일에 뛰어들어 경제적 자립을 이루겠다고 결심했다. 이후 10년 동안 그녀는 '익스프레스', '미러', '데일리 메일' 등에 런던 젊은 상류층 사회의 은밀한 가십 기사를 기고했다.

당시는 오늘날 파자마 파티와 유럽 대륙으로의 한밤중 드라이브로 점철된 광란의 시대로 자주 묘사되는 '브라이트 영 씽즈(Bright Young Things)'의 세상이었다. 그러나 카틀랜드의 칼럼을 들여다보면 여전히 제1차 세계대전의 충격에서 헤어나오지 못한 사회의 실상이 고스란히 드러난다. 아버지들은 전사했고(카틀랜드 역시 1918년 참호 속에서 아버지를 잃었다), 유서 깊은 대저택들은 매각되었으며, 이혼은 도처에 널려 있었고 술이나 약물 없이는 삶을 버텨내기 힘들어 보였다. 카틀랜드가 교제했던 남성들은 훗날 그녀가 소설 속에 써내려간 심장을 뛰게 만드는 공작이나 용맹한 비행사가 아니라, 자신의 참담한 황폐함을 표현할 언어조차 갖지 못한 부서진 영혼들이었다. '내 또래들은 감정을 드러내는 것을 부끄러워했다'고 그녀는 1943년 회고록 『지협의 시절들(The Isthmus Years)』에서 날카롭게 회고했다. '우리 모두는 동정을 끔찍이도 두려워했다.'

그리하여 그녀는 상황을 최선으로 이끌겠다는 바스러질 듯 팽팽한 결의를 품고 묵묵히 전진했다. 핑고 랭그리시나 닉스 라텐던 같은 기이한 이름을 가진 남성들과 수많은 염문을 뿌린 끝에, 그녀는 인쇄업 재벌의 후계자였던 무미건조한 남성 알렉산더 맥코쿼데일과 정략결혼을 감행했다. 그가 아버지와 마찬가지로 술에 빠져들자, 그녀는 이혼 후 곧바로 그의 사촌 형제와 재혼하는 영리한 맞바꿈을 단행했다. 이로써 성(姓)을 바꿀 필요도 없었다. 한 명의 맥코쿼데일 씨를 또 다른 맥코쿼데일 씨로 대체했을 뿐이었다. 1991년 스스로 데임(Dame, 여성 기사 작위) 작위를 받을 때까지 귀족 작위를 얻지 못했던 것은 그녀의 가슴에 응어리로 남았다. 반면 그녀의 야심만만한 딸 레인은 치밀하게 계산된 세 번의 결혼을 통해 번번이 귀족 사회의 최상류층에 당당히 입성했다.

카틀랜드에게 진정으로 소중했던 유일한 남성은 사랑하는 남동생 로널드뿐이었다. 두 사람은 함께 휴가를 떠나고 1920년대에 대유행했던 사이비 동양 철학에 대해 끝없는 대화를 나누었다. 우스펜스키와 구르디예프가 그들이 가장 좋아했던 사상가였으며, 카틀랜드는 유령과 영적 치유를 믿는 모호한 신비주의를 임종 때까지 간직했다. 그녀는 비행접시(UFO)의 존재를 믿었고, 꿀이 거의 모든 질병을 고칠 수 있다고 맹신하기도 했다.

남매는 정치, 특히 사회 참여적이고 국제주의적인 토리당(보수당) 노선을 통해서도 깊은 유대감을 형성했다. 바버라는 로널드를 닦달하여 의회에 진출시켰고, 그는 대독 융화 정책에 앞장서 반대하는 유력 정치인으로 성장했다. 바버라 역시 나치 정권의 반유대주의적 악행을 정면으로 다룬 1930년대 영국 소설의 극소수 선구자 중 한 편을 집필했다. 1936년작 소설 『위험한 실험(Dangerous Experiment)』은 난파를 겪고 코카서스의 뇌우 숭배 부족에게 노예로 붙잡혔다가 독일로 흘러들어가 나치 장교 애인의 구애를 받게 되는 레나 캐링턴의 황당무계한 모험을 다룬다. 결국 주인공은 그 장교가 유대인 피난민을 가혹하게 학대하는 모습을 목격하고 결별을 선언한다.

물론 이는 1980년대 이후 우리 대다수가 기억하는 바버라 카틀랜드의 모습과는 거리가 멀다. 스위트가 '제국주의적 전성기'라 칭한 이 시기에 그녀는 종잇장처럼 얄팍한 줄거리를 끊임없이 재활용하며 소설을 찍어냈다. 또한 집요할 정도로 자기 PR에 열을 올렸다. 침구, 양초, 수건 등이 모두 그녀의 이름을 내걸고 열성적으로 팔려나갔지만, 놀라운 절제력을 발휘하여 향기 나는 화장지만큼은 상품화를 거부했다. 또한 정육점 체인 듀허스트와 손잡고 손님들이 12파운드를 소비할 때마다 미출간 카틀랜드 소설 6편 중 한 권을 증정하는 공동 마케팅을 성사시키기도 했다. 하지만 '다진 소고기 뭉치와 함께 소설 『사막의 욕망』 한 권을 받아드는' 상황의 극심한 기괴함 탓에 이 행사는 그리 큰 성공을 거두지 못했다.

그러나 지금 돌이켜보아도 비현실적으로 느껴질 만큼 믿기 힘든 행운이 찾아왔다. 그녀의 딸 레인이 다이애나 스펜서(다이애나 왕세자비)의 의붓어머니가 되자, 카틀랜드는 황실과 자신의 브랜드를 교차 번식시킬 절호의 기회를 감지했다. 그녀는 '처녀성은 내가 발명한 것'이라고 공언하고 다녔으며, 1981년 세기의 왕실 결혼식에 정작 초대받지 못했음에도 그 결혼이 마치 자신의 공로인 양 넌지시 암시하곤 했다. 어머니의 피를 그대로 물려받은 딸 레인은 스펜서 가문의 본택인 올소프의 기념품점에서 바버라 카틀랜드의 전작 시리즈를 전면 진열해 판매하도록 조치했다.

카틀랜드를 단지 한 시대의 기행이자 두 번 다시 보지 못할 별종으로 치부해 버리는 것은 손쉬운 일일 것이다. 그러나 이 탁월한 평전이 거둔 위대한 성취는, 스위트가 그녀를 20세기의 경제적·정치적·사회적·예술적 대변혁 속에 확고히 위치시키는 동시에 그녀가 어떻게 그 시대의 한계를 초월해 나갔는지를 치밀하게 추적했다는 점에 있다. 어찌 되었든, 그리고 이것이 여전히 풀리지 않는 심오한 신비로 남아 있는 한, 바버라 카틀랜드는 진정 감탄할 만한 하나의 상징으로 우뚝 선다. 바로 완벽하게 자신의 힘으로 스스로를 창조해 낸 자수성가형 여성(self-made woman)이라는 사실이다.

2026-08-25.title: ‘It looked stunning on Joanna Lumley!’: 10 writers on their biggest hair disaster
2026-08-25.author: Kate Lloyd, Rich Pelley, Jeffrey Ingold, Carys Afoko, Joel Snape, Viv Groskop, Paula Cocozza, Polly Hudson, Daniel Lavelle and Alexi Duggins
paragraphs: From bowl cuts to extreme mullets, punk dos to bad dye jobs, a terrible hairstyle can never be forgotten – even decades after it has grown out

It’s the late 1990s. Big, round, feathered fringes are a huge deal at my primary school. Most of my friends have one, influenced by Britney Spears or Emma Bunton. I, too, have a fringe. Mine, as you can see, appears more inspired by Kevin Keegan circa 1993.

Of course, calling what I’m sporting here “a fringe” is an incredible understatement. If you squint it could be a trendy east London mullet. Otherwise, I look a bit like a Knight Templar. Or someone wearing a hat made out of their own hair, on top of their own hair.

It may surprise you to learn this cut was not the result of a sleepover prank gone wrong. It was done by a professional – a hairdresser who lived up the road from my parents and came round to our house to cut my brother’s, my mum’s and my hair.

When I first discovered these photos, I assumed the look must have been a one-off. Maybe I moved just as the hairdresser was trimming the top and the only way to salvage things was to evoke Pat Sharp. Or maybe it was the hair equivalent of that botched Jesus fresco restoration: every attempt to improve it only made it worse.

It turns out I actually wore this hairstyle for almost a year, according to my mum. I have a photo of me in a summer dress – with a forehead that resembles a city skyline – where I’m probably seven. And there’s another where I’m wearing a primary school jumper, aged eight.
My mum has no recollection of the hair being a problem. She was happy with the cut back then, she says. “You were a little girl!” is her defence now.

Thankfully, I have no memory of actually sporting it. I have, however, spent most of my adult life feeling disproportionately stressed about going to the hairdresser. As they say, the body keeps the score. Kate Lloyd

They say you don’t appreciate something until you lose it – and that is never more true than with hair. After decades of treating mine as a disposable fashion accessory, it appears to have disposed of itself. Perhaps that’s why I look back so fondly on all the terrible things I did to it while I still had the chance.

The first was a pudding-bowl haircut that my mum and I appeared to share in the early 80s. At school, I had shoulder-length curtains with a shaved undercut, held out of my face with an alice band – a look I imagined made me resemble a member of Radiohead, rather than a teenage girl waiting to wash her face. It required constant maintenance because the curtains had to fall at exactly the right angle: too far apart and you looked like a medieval monk, too close together and you couldn’t see where you were going.

At college, it was a number one all over with a line shaved through one eyebrow, like Robbie Williams in Take That – or so I believed. I thought it made me look dangerous. In reality, I resembled someone who had lost a brief but intense argument with an electric razor.

At university, I had dreadlocks that made me look like Sonic the Hedgehog. For my first proper job, I went bleached blond, which accidentally made me look like my mum again, so that had to go. Then came a spiky mohawk: less Mr T, more startled parrot.

The problem is that, for the people around me, the dramatic effect diminishes each time. When I brilliantly shaved the top half of my head to look like Keith Flint from the Prodigy for a 90s-themed fancy-dress party, nowhere near enough people said: “I can’t believe what you’ve done to your hair!” Or: “You’ve won first prize.” Instead, they presumably thought: “What has Rich done to his hair now? What a berk.”

That, out of all the haircuts, was probably my worst, although it faces extremely stiff competition. Unlike my other terrible hairstyles, this one had only ever been intended to last for one night. The next morning, my Keith Flint costume had gone back in the wardrobe, but unfortunately my hair remained the same, so I was forced into another brief but intense argument with an electric razor – and this time the razor won. I thought I looked like Jay-Z, but in reality I looked more like an escaped convict. Rich Pelley

Meet Jeff at age 15 in 2006. Yes, you can laugh. I’d honestly be insulted if you didn’t laugh. My hair looks like a cross between a bird’s nest and tumbleweed. I believe the technical term for it is a “terrible mess”.

For about three years as a young teenager, I outright refused to get a haircut and just let my hair run wild. I would roll out of bed and without even so much as looking at a comb or a brush, walk out the door with an unkempt, knotty mess on my head.

I wasn’t trying to be edgy or cool. Believe me, I was teased mercilessly for my bad hair. Kids would come up and ask if there was something living in there or complain to the teacher that my hair was a distraction in class. Or they would “joke” that my parents were so poor they couldn’t afford to get me a haircut. One day when I was walking home from school, a group of students tried to throw pieces of chewed gum into my hair.
Still, I stubbornly brushed off any suggestions I should go to the hairdressers. That hairstyle was a masterclass in deflection and adolescent survival.

The summer before I started secondary school, a small group of classmates had spread a rumour that I was gay. News to me at the time. I didn’t even know what “gay” meant except it was clearly something bad and shameful. Friends whom I would once play with in the streets shunned me. No one would return my calls to hang out.

It was then that I decided to grow my hair. I walked into that first day of secondary school with the beginnings of my unruly, curly mane. I was almost unrecognisable to those who’d known me for years with an outdated mushroom cut.

The classroom whispers about my sexuality were drowned out by incessant questions and commentary about my ever-growing untamed hair. I didn’t know much back then, but something told me it was better to be the kid with weird hair than it was to be the gay kid. My hair became my armour.

I wore it proudly and only cut it when I got accepted to university in my final year of school. By then it reached the top of my chest. I could see the light at the end of a dark, lonely tunnel. I was finally getting out of my small town and going somewhere no one knew me. I no longer needed to hide behind my hair. Though the kids were right: I am gay. Jeffrey Ingold

Cast your mind back to June 2011. Beyoncé took to the Pyramid stage at Glastonbury for a historic performance. She was resplendent in a gold-sequinned cardigan and black ankle boots and had a cascade of honey blond curls. I had blagged my way to a bar job at the festival to see my idol and I was not disappointed. It was a near-religious experience. As I began the long trek home from Worthy farm in Pilton, Somerset, I knew one thing: I had to dye my hair blond.

I had attempted to dye my hair at home once, with disastrous results. This time, I made my way to a salon in east London with a picture of Beyoncé on my phone. My hairdresser, a lovely New Zealander called Vernon, understood the vision, and within a couple of hours I had been transformed. So began a summer to remember. My honey blond curls and I went to more festivals, parties and art openings than I had ever gone to before. Blonds, I decided, did have more fun.

Blond, it turned out, was also more work. My hair was weaker and drier than usual. It took only a couple of months for my very dark roots to peep through, then I was back to the salon to see Vernon. After a few months I noticed the warm, honey colour was morphing into something more brassy. A friend explained that I needed a special shampoo to maintain the colour, maybe even a toner. I bought a £4 purple shampoo from Boots and hoped for the best. I was already shelling out to get my roots done. I wasn’t made of money.

The breaking point came after a two-week beach holiday. One minute I was sipping rum out of a coconut, the next the tropical sun had bleached my curls white blond. I barely wore sunscreen in those days; it hadn’t occurred to me to protect my hair. It wasn’t the look I was going for, but I liked it, until I went back to see Vernon.
“Babe, we can’t bleach it any more. The condition is terrible,” he said, running his fingers through my fried curls. Instead, he cut my hair and sent me on my way with dark roots and a broken spirit.

Over the months that followed I endured the worst hair days of my life, growing out the blond and returning to my natural dark brown. My hair broke easily and I learned the hard way that colouring your hair is a commitment: the only low-maintenance way to have blond hair is to be born with it. Carys Afoko

It’s hard to remember, in our post-God-of-War, post-Jeff-Bridges-from-Iron-Man era, that growing a massive beard, if you’re bald, was once not considered the cranial topiary slam-dunk it’s now assumed to be. Back when Shrek 2 was the hottest thing at the box office, skinhead-plus-facial-bush had a faint whiff of desperation about it. It looked a bit villainous, and opened you up to comparisons with those toys where you use a tiny magnet to drag iron filings across an eerily hairless man’s face. I simply wasn’t prepared to risk it.

And so, dear reader, I experimented. Forced to shave my head in my early 20s after losing most of my hair terrifyingly prematurely, I riffled through a variety of looks. I tried stubble, I tried shorter beards, I tried the Van Dyke – named after the 17th-century Flemish painter Anthony van Dyck, whose subjects often sported the same sort of chin-patch. Think Cyrus the Virus, the baddie from Con Air. Once, in a dating profile, I tried a big hat (I am, I should say to any ladies who felt misled when I showed up, sincerely sorry). And then I tried this.

Quite honestly, I don’t know what I was going for here, with what I believe is technically an extended goatee. Stage magician? High-end jewel thief? Futuristic pirate? I do remember that around this time I wrote a feature where I went undercover in a group of pickup artists, and so maybe their penchant for “peacocking” (having something distinct and memorable about one’s appearance, even if it’s ridiculous) rubbed off on me. It certainly draws the eye, like a bluebottle on a birthday cake. I just can’t believe I thought it looked good.

In this photo, I’m at a press event on a boat in 2003. Within hours of getting back to shore, I also came back down to earth: reminded by friends and flatmates that having a head like an egg is still preferable to looking like someone Jason Bourne would threaten to throw off a balcony.

The good thing about beards is that you can experiment with impunity: I got rid of this one the morning afterwards, and stuck to the full buzz cut – no facial topiary in sight – until the late 2010s. That’s when the beard plus bald combo started really coming into its own. With the odd blip for Halloween outfits, I’ve had a full-bore beard ever since: they’re perfect for the shaving-averse, and surprisingly easy to shape.

In a sense, I’m very lucky – I have friends who’ve gradually gone just as bald as me over the intervening decade, but remain unable to grow more than the wispiest facial fuzz. And so, to any twentysomethings staring at their emerging scalp with horror right now, I’d like to say: keep the faith, it will improve, as long as you can grow a proper beard. Just don’t forget what Jeff Bridges did for us. Joel Snape

Everyone knows that it’s a bad idea to get your hair cut on the same day that you are having your photograph taken. This picture operates as a public health reminder of this fact. On a personal level it also illustrates why virtually no one is ever allowed to cut my hair. In 40-plus years of adult life, only three hairdressers have gained sufficient trust to be allowed to use scissors in my vicinity. You can see why.

This photograph must have been taken around 1977, when I was about three or four. I remember the photographer coming to set up at the house. Most people didn’t own cameras, and photographer home visits were just one of the exceptionally weird “normal things” people did in the 1970s.

Another key recollection I have from around that time is an overriding fear of the Daleks and of Tom Baker (who was then the Doctor in Doctor Who). The photograph was taken in the room that housed the place where terror resided: the television. Now, a new, chilling dimension was added to the horror already contained within those four walls: the immortalisation of this haircut.

This was the era of the fashionable “Purdey” or “pageboy” cut. It looked stunning on Joanna Lumley in The New Avengers. It was slightly less stunning on a moody toddler old enough to know how awful she looked but too young to do anything about it. Around this age, I must have learned about the idea of bowl haircuts: a cut-price, kitchen-table haircut achieved by putting a bowl on someone’s head and cutting around it. I knew I looked as if I had one.

The truth, however, was worse. A professional hairdresser did this in a salon and my parents paid money for it. I recently asked my mum for more details of this historic misdemeanor and she replied: “It was done very badly.” You think? Viv Groskop

When I was 10, I decided to do the unthinkable. I asked my parents for short hair. Being a girl, this went against the traditional beauty ideals I was growing up with in my family. As a child of the 70s, I had artless long hair and no fringe. One of my happiest childhood memories is of sitting on my dad’s lap on Saturday evenings after my weekly hair wash and having him comb and dry my hair while we watched Starsky & Hutch.

But I was increasingly fashion-conscious. I found a picture of a model with the hair I wanted, and tore it out of our Freemans mail order catalogue. She had a fringe and a brunette version of the style made famous by Diana, Princess of Wales, with slightly less layering.

We picked the salon for practical reasons. It was halfway between school and home, in a parade of shops next to a chemist and a butcher’s. Mum took me in with my picture. We showed it to the hairdresser, who looked at it and nodded. I sat in the chair and soon chunks of long brown hair began to land on the floor.
